body.text:
Ce catalysed BZ oscillator lab notes with listed concentrations, stirred at 25 C, target period ~60 s. Does the 2-variable reduction keep the period here?
NaBrO3 0.06 M (sodium bromate concentration)
malonic acid 0.02 M (malonic acid concentration)
H2SO4 -> [H+] 0.8 M (acid hydrogen ion concentration)
Ce(IV), stirred, 25 C (catalyst and conditions)
period ~ 60 s +- 10 s (target oscillation period)

nodes.title: Full model oscillates for this recipe
nodes.statement: The full three-variable Oregonator derived from the listed bromate, malonic acid and acid concentrations oscillates as a limit cycle, with colour changes repeating every full cycle.
nodes.rationale: Without a limit cycle in the full 3-variable model there is no period to preserve or to compare with 60 s.

check.description: Run stiff Oregonator solver derived from recipe; passes if a stable limit cycle is found.
check.question: oscillates

nodes.title: Reduction preserves the period
nodes.statement: The two-variable Oregonator reduction keeps the same oscillation period as the full model for this recipe within 15 percent.
nodes.rationale: This is the asked question: quasi-steady-state reduction can shift the period even when oscillation persists.

check.description: Run full versus 2-variable Oregonator solvers for this recipe; passes if relative period difference is within tolerance.
check.question: reduction_keeps_period

nodes.title: Full-cycle period hits the 60-second target
nodes.statement: The full-model oscillation period in seconds, measured between consecutive maxima, lies within 10 seconds of 60 seconds.
nodes.rationale: The lab goal is a 60 s colour-change cycle; a model that oscillates at a very different speed does not meet the goal.

check.description: Computed full-cycle period in seconds compared with target; engine computes the period from the solver.

nodes.title: Stirring keeps the mixture uniform
nodes.statement: Stirring keeps the solution spatially uniform so a well-mixed Oregonator without diffusion describes the lab beaker.
nodes.rationale: Unstirred gradients, waves and diffusion would invalidate comparison of beaker colour period with an ODE period.

nodes.title: Temperature stays at 25 degrees for rate constants
nodes.statement: The mixture stays near 25 degrees during oscillation so the rate constants used to convert the recipe to model time remain valid.
nodes.rationale: Field-Noyes rate constants and the seconds-per-model-time conversion depend strongly on temperature and acid conditions.

nodes.title: Cerium stoichiometric factor stays in oscillatory range
nodes.statement: The cerium-catalysed stoichiometric factor remains in the oscillatory window for the whole run without catalyst loss changing it.
nodes.rationale: Cerium cycling, carbon dioxide bubble loss and reactant consumption can move the effective stoichiometric factor out of the oscillatory window.

body.summary: Read as testing the stated Ce-catalysed stirred recipe against the Oregonator, not fitting a new recipe to hit 60 s. The tree first checks full-model oscillation and the 2-variable period error, then whether that full-cycle period meets 60 s plus or minus 10 s.

body.reason: Small eps, very small q and eps_prime give timescale separation and s=1 lies inside the classic oscillatory window, so a stable limit cycle is expected.
epsilon_prime is ~500x smaller than epsilon so Y is strongly fast and its quasi-steady elimination introduces negligible period error.

body.question: The period misses the 60 s target. Which recipe change would bring it there, and what would that risk for the reduction?
body.answer: VIBloom computed the miss for the listed recipe. My reasoning is that raising malonic acid shortens the time scale and so should lower the period. My reasoning is that it also raises eps and eps_prime, risking the separation that lets reduction hold. The tree does not compute that trade-off yet, so open full-oscillates next with higher malonic acid.

body.reason: With q tiny and eps_prime << eps the x-z reduced Jacobian has positive trace, making the steady state unstable and producing a limit cycle.
With eps_prime ~2e-4 much smaller than eps ~0.1 the fast-variable quasi-steady approximation is well separated so period error should stay under 15%.

candidates.explanation: Reduction fails because activator relaxation is not fast relative to inhibitor growth so the reduced flow shortens the oscillation period.
candidates.scope: Recipes where timescale separation sets period error while excitability threshold remains regular.

candidates.explanation: Reduction fails because small excitation threshold sharpens the activator nullcline so elimination of the fast intermediate shortens the refractory phase.
candidates.scope: Recipes where excitation threshold sharpness sets period error independent of activator inhibitor timescale separation.

body.open: A single test cannot establish the range of recipes over which the supported mechanism holds.
